Figure 1. Schematic representation of the possible steps in the metabolism of aerobic methanotrophic bacteria. O2 is used in the oxidation of CH4 to methanol in the first step catalyzed by MMO enzymes (represented by the pMMO in this scheme). This first step may also be performed in the cytoplasm by the sMMO in methanotrophic bacteria possessing this enzyme. Methanol is converted to formaldehyde by methanol dehydrogenase (MDH); formaldehyde can be assimilated into cellular compounds (via the ribulose monophosphate (RuMP) cycle in gammaproteobacterial MOB or via the serine cycle in alphaproteobacterial MOB) or be oxidized to formate by formaldehyde dehydrogenases (FADH); formate is then oxidized to CO2 by formate dehydrogenases (FDH). O2 is the terminal electron acceptor in aerobic respiration, while other oxidants can potentially serve as terminal electron acceptors in methanotrophic bacteria performing anaerobic respiration under O2-limiting conditions. Under O2 limitation, carbon that enters the RuMP cycle can go through fermentation for energy generation as opposed to respiration. ∗Iron (Fe3+) and manganese (Mn4+) reduction would presumably occur outside the cell, via extracellular electron transfer, and could potentially be mediated by electron shuttles or microbial consortia. This figure was created with BioRender.

Fig. 1. Redox balancing strategies used by PNSB during anaerobic photoheterotrophic growth on a reduced carbon source. During photoheterotrophic growth of PNSB on butyrate, ATP is produced by cyclic photophosphorylation, in which electrons are repeatedly energized by light, allowing them to be cycled through a proton-pumping electron transport chain, rather than being transferred to a terminal electron acceptor. Thus, PNSB must use other means to dispose of extra electrons that are generated during use of a carbon source like butyrate, which is more reduced than biomass (Table 1). Three mechanisms are depicted: (A) CO2 ﬁxation via the Calvin cycle; (B) H2 production via nitrogenase (N2ase; green arrow); and (C) DMSO reduction by DMSO reductase (DMSOR; red arrow). Solid black lines, carbon metabolism; solid blue lines, energy metabolism; dotted lines, electron metabolism.

Fig. 3 | Mechanisms for electron transport across the outer surface. Models for the porin–cytochrome system found in Gram-​negative bacteria (part a), the cytochrome-​based system in Gram-​positive bacteria (part b), the cytochrome-​based system in archaea (part c) and the flavoprotein-​based system in Gram-​positive bacteria (part d). Electrons derived from electron donor oxidation within the cell are typically transferred to lipophilic, quinone-​based electron carriers, such as menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone (DMK), or in the case of some archaea possibly to membrane-​bound proteins such as Rnf complexes. In many systems, one or more c-​type cytochromes route electrons to the outer surface. Additional c-​type cytochromes displayed on the outer cell surface can provide additional electrical contacts for electron transfer to electron acceptors. Gram-​positive bacteria that lack c-​type cytochromes rely on flavoproteins, which transfer electrons to chelated Fe(III) or flavins (represented by hexagons) that can diffuse through the cell wall. The subscripts ox and red in parts a–d refer to oxidized and reduced, respectively.
